messages.subject: automatic differentiation documentation
parts:
Hi,
I am new to Stan and thanks for the excellent work. I want to use the automatic differentiation module in Stan for my neural network research. Unfortunately I could not find a tutorial or similar documentation for auto-diff in Stan manual. I have read some parts of the code, and I have some questions. If there exists a tutorial or similar documentation, could you share it with me ? Thanks, best regards,

Yusuf

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] automatic differentiation documentation
parts:
There is no tutorial yet on how to use autodiff standalone.

What I would recommend is looking at src/stan/agrad/autodiff.hpp
to see if you can use the top-level functionals. Those will autodiff
any functor with a vector argument. The list of available functions
is pretty much what's documented in the Stan manual.

If that's not fine-grained enough control for you, I'd recommend
looking inside the implementations in autodiff.hpp, which provide
pretty simple examples of how to use the lower-level functionality.

There are also extensive unit tests in src/test/unit/agrad.

In Stan 2.4, the gradients are complete, but not the higher-order
autodiff. They should be complete for 2.5.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] automatic differentiation documentation
parts:
Here’s a simple example,

#include <iostream>
#include <time.h>

#include <stan/model/model_header.hpp>
#include <stan/model/util.hpp>

struct funnel_func {

  template <typename T>
  T operator()(Eigen::Matrix<T, Eigen::Dynamic, 1>& x) const {
    const int N = 100;

    

    T v = x[0];

    T y[N];
    for (int n = 0; n < N; ++n)
      y[n] = x[n + 1];

    T sum_x2 = 0;

    for (int n = 0; n < N; ++n)
      sum_x2 += square(y[n]);

    T p1 = 0.5 * N * v;

    

    T p2 = 0.5 * sum_x2 * exp(-v);

    

    T p3 = 0.5 * square(v) / 9.0;

    return p1 + p2 + p3;
  }
};


int main(int argc, const char * argv[]) {

  clock_t start;
  clock_t end;
  double deltaT;

  

  int n_calls = 5000;

  //////////////////////////////////////////////////
  //              Funnel Test Function            //
  //////////////////////////////////////////////////

  Eigen::VectorXd x = Eigen::VectorXd::Ones(101);
  Eigen::VectorXd v = Eigen::VectorXd::Ones(101);
  Eigen::MatrixXd M = Eigen::MatrixXd::Identity(101, 101);

  double f;
  Eigen::VectorXd grad(x.size());
  Eigen::MatrixXd hessian(x.size(), x.size());
  Eigen::VectorXd grad_m_times_h(x.size());

  funnel_func funnel;

  // First-order timing
  start = clock();
  for (int n = 0; n < 100 * n_calls; ++n)
    stan::agrad::gradient(funnel, x, f, grad);
  end = clock();

  

  deltaT = (double)(end - start) / CLOCKS_PER_SEC;

  

  std::cout << 100 * n_calls << " gradients took " << deltaT << " seconds" << std::endl;

  

  // Second-order timing
  start = clock();
  for (int n = 0; n < n_calls; ++n)
    stan::agrad::hessian<double>(funnel, x, f, grad, hessian);
  end = clock();

  

  deltaT = (double)(end - start) / CLOCKS_PER_SEC;

  

  std::cout << n_calls << " hessians took " << deltaT << " seconds" << std::endl;

  

  start = clock();
  for (int n = 0; n < n_calls; ++n)
    stan::agrad::grad_tr_mat_times_hessian(funnel, x, M, grad_m_times_h);
  end = clock();

  

  deltaT = (double)(end - start) / CLOCKS_PER_SEC;

  

  std::cout << n_calls << " grad-matrix-times-hessians took " << deltaT << " seconds" << std::endl;

  return 0;

}

parts:
Hi,
Thanks for the answers. Using top-level functions does not seem appropriate for me. Both parameters (weights of layers and biases) and inputs will be matrices in my case. I want to have classes that have member variables (the parameters of the neural networks) of type Eigen::Matrix( stan::agrad::var, Eigen::Dynamic, Eigen Dynamic) or its vector form for the biases. As far as I understand, Stan uses a memory pool and puts all of the chainable variables in a global variable (var_stack_ defined in stan/agrad/rev/var_stack.cpp) and all the top level functions call recover_memory() function and gives the allocated memory back to the pool. Reconstructing the whole neural network at each gradient evaluation seems too costly. So instead of calling them I need to call the static function stan::agrad::grad(chainable *vi) on the final cost variable of my neural net (which will be of type stan::agrad::var) and call the recover_memory() function only in the destructor of my classes. Now the problem is if I have more than one neural net object in a single program, their parameters will be put in the same global stack, and when I take gradient for one (or destruct it), the other will also be effected. What I need is a separate stack (and maybe a separate pool) for each of my objects. Is that possible? Thanks, best regards,

Yusuf

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] automatic differentiation documentation
parts:
The stack is global, so it's not really possible to reuse.
We're about to roll out a version that allows local autodiff
to be done on top of the stack without disrupting the bottom ---
we need that for our diff eq solver that autodiffs an ode
system before passing it to an integrator as part of a sampling
or optimization step.

You can make the stack thread local if your
autodiff arises from multiple threads. That worked when we last
tested it, but that was quite a while ago.

- Bob
